lines: Former Viking Global investor Paul Enright argues that analyzing a business and picking a stock are separate disciplines: a great company only becomes a good trade once valuation, liquidity, factor exposure and market expectations are factored in.

He describes portfolio management as an 'accordion', actively flexing gross and net exposure with the strength of available spreads and reallocating capital to the highest-conviction ideas like setting a baseball lineup.
On shorts, Enright layers offensive bets against weak businesses, relative-value shorts paired with longs and market-proxy hedges, while respecting liquidity limits to avoid bear traps.
He says rebalancing should hinge on whether a price move reflects changed fundamental expectations or noise, and sees the best setups where revenue inflects without a matching rise in costs.
Enright notes passive capital and large multi-manager platforms have made large-cap alpha harder to find, and closes with personal frameworks such as a growth mindset and regret minimization.
podcast: Capital Allocators – Inside the Institutional Investment Industry
title: [REPLAY] Paul Enright – Inside Long-Short Equity Investing (Capital Allocators, EP.266)
